meta.audience: The people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi and the Nephites of Zarahemla
meta.location: The land of Nephi, the wilderness, Zarahemla, Jershon
meta.unit: The sons of Mosiah among the Lamanites (Alma 17–26)

world_behind.title: The second slaughter has no war behind it
world_behind.text: Verse 2 says the Amalekites, unable to reach the Nephites, turned on the converts again. The killing in this chapter is displaced anger with nothing left to aim at.

world_behind.title: The converts do not defend themselves twice
world_behind.text: Verse 3 says they again refused arms and again let themselves be killed. Alma 24 established the covenant; this chapter shows it holding under a second test.

world_behind.title: The king expects the Nephites to kill them
world_behind.text: Verse 6 has him name the reason plainly: many murders and sins committed against those people. His fear is a correct assessment of what he deserves.

world_behind.title: He offers slavery and Ammon refuses it
world_behind.text: Verses 8 and 9 have the king propose that his nation serve as slaves until the debt is repaid, and Ammon answer that Nephite law forbids it. Mosiah 2 has Benjamin saying the same thing about his own reign.

world_behind.title: Ammon inquires before he moves
world_behind.text: Verse 7 offers the test and verse 11 carries it out. The exodus of a whole nation waits on a question actually asked.

world_behind.title: The admission goes to a vote
world_behind.text: Verse 21 has the chief judge send a proclamation asking for the voice of the people. A national immigration decision is put to the assembly, and verse 22 is its answer.

world_behind.title: The terms are stated in the same breath as the welcome
world_behind.text: Verse 24 grants Jershon and armies to guard it, on condition that the newcomers fund those armies out of their substance. Generosity and a bill arrive together.

words.text: To make restitution, to pay back what was destroyed. The record uses the word four times and the King James Bible fourteen, where it almost always means fixing the temple. The king proposes to repair many murders by giving his nation into service.

One who seeks. The noun occurs once in scripture. Mormon uses it to name who gets the kind of joy that put Ammon on the ground: the truly penitent and humble seeker of happiness, which makes the joy a consequence of a search rather than an accident.

The land granted to the converts, on the east by the sea and south of Bountiful. It appears twenty-six times, all in Alma. The record never translates the name, and the land becomes the front line of the war in Alma 43.

Property, what a person owns. The record uses the word twenty-seven times, most often in Mosiah 4 and Alma 1 about giving to the poor. Here it names the tax that pays for the army protecting the people who will not fight.

Loathing, revulsion. The word appears twice in this record and never in the King James Bible; the other use is Alma 13, of sin itself. Here the people of Ammon look on shedding blood the way Alma 13 looks on wickedness.

A curved sword. It occurs three times in this record, in Enos, here, and in Alma 44, and never in the King James Bible. Mormon names it beside the sword to say the refusal covered every weapon they had.

phrases.term: They were treated as though they were angels sent from God
phrases.text: Mormon explains why Ammon and his brethren could not stand to watch. The converts loved them and had received them as messengers. The compassion in the verse runs on a relationship built over fourteen years.

phrases.term: The Nephites will destroy us, because of the many murders and sins we have committed
phrases.text: The king's objection to the rescue plan. He is not arguing that the charge is false. He assumes the people he wronged will act on it, and Ammon has to test the assumption before anyone moves.

phrases.term: We will be their slaves until we repair unto them
phrases.text: The king's opening offer for asylum. He proposes to hand over the liberty of a nation as compensation, which is the measure of how he weighs what they did.

phrases.term: It is against the law of our brethren... that there should be any slaves among them
phrases.text: Ammon refuses the offer on legal grounds. A Nephite prince tells a Lamanite king that his own country will not take what is being offered, and redirects him to rely on mercy instead.

phrases.term: Satan has great hold on the hearts of the Amalekites
phrases.text: The Lord's own reading of the situation, given as the reason to leave. The instruction is to get out, and the assessment of the enemy comes attached to it rather than a promise of protection in place.

phrases.term: We will try the hearts of our brethren
phrases.text: Ammon leaves an entire nation camped in the wilderness while he goes to find out whether they are welcome. The test is of Nephite hearts, and the record uses the same verb it uses for assaying metal.

phrases.term: Joy which none receiveth save it be the truly penitent and humble seeker of happiness
phrases.text: Mormon interrupts the narrative to say who this kind of joy is for. The qualification matches Alma 26, where the penitent are the ones who can know. Joy and knowledge are put behind the same door.

phrases.term: Their joy was not that to exceed their strength
phrases.text: Mormon notes that Alma, Aaron, Omner, and Himni stayed on their feet. The observation is almost dry, and it makes Ammon's collapse a fact about Ammon rather than a general rule.

phrases.term: Desiring the voice of the people concerning the admitting their brethren
phrases.text: The chief judge puts a question of national admission to a vote. The reign of the judges is nine chapters old, and this is what Mosiah's reform looks like operating on something difficult.

phrases.term: On condition that they will give us a portion of their substance
phrases.text: The Nephites attach a price to the protection. They will guard a people who will not fight, and the people who will not fight will pay for the guarding. The record puts the arrangement on paper without comment.

phrases.term: Death was swallowed up to them by the victory of Christ over it
phrases.text: Paul's sentence from 1 Corinthians 15, applied to a nation that has decided to be killed rather than kill. Mormon gives the doctrine as the reason they could hold the covenant.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: The killing resumes
verses.text: The Lamanite armies give up on the Nephites and go home. The Amalekites, angry at the loss, stir the people against the converts again. The converts refuse arms a second time and are slain.

verses.label: v. 4–10
verses.title: The plan
verses.text: Ammon and his brethren, moved with compassion, propose flight to Zarahemla. The king objects that the Nephites will kill them for what they did, offers to go as slaves, and is told Nephite law forbids slavery. He agrees to go if the Lord says go.

verses.label: v. 11–14
verses.title: The answer, and the departure
verses.text: The Lord tells Ammon to get the people out, names Satan's hold on the Amalekites, and promises preservation. They gather the whole nation with flocks and herds and camp in the wilderness between the two lands.

verses.label: v. 15–19
verses.title: The meeting
verses.text: Ammon leaves them there and goes to test Nephite hearts. He meets Alma, and the joy takes his strength and puts him on the ground. Mormon says this joy belongs to the penitent, and notes that the other three stayed standing.

verses.label: v. 20–24
verses.title: The vote
verses.text: Alma brings them to his own house and to the chief judge. A proclamation goes out for the voice of the people. The answer grants Jershon, promises armies between Jershon and Nephi, and sets the condition that the newcomers help pay for them.

verses.label: v. 25–27
verses.title: Jershon, and a name
verses.text: Ammon and Alma carry the answer back to the tents; Alma tells them his own conversion story. They take possession of Jershon, are called the people of Ammon, and are numbered with the church of God.

verses.label: v. 28–30
verses.title: What they became
verses.text: Abhorrence of bloodshed, no persuading them to arms, no terror at death because of their hope in Christ and the resurrection. They would die in the worst way inflicted before drawing sword or cimeter, and Mormon calls them highly favored.

chapter.title: The covenant is tested a second time and holds
chapter.text: Alma 24 could be read as a single decision under pressure. Alma 27 shows the same people making it again, with the outcome already known, and Mormon records both refusals.

chapter.title: The rescue is proposed by the people who converted them
chapter.text: Ammon's brethren see the destruction of men who received them as angels and move to get them out. The mission ends in evacuation logistics.

chapter.title: The king's guilt is accurate and it still does not decide the case
chapter.text: He is right about what his people did. Ammon takes the fear seriously enough to inquire, and the answer is to go anyway and rely on mercy.

chapter.title: Slavery is refused by the country being offered it
chapter.text: The king volunteers his nation and Ammon cites law against it. The record treats the prohibition as settled Nephite policy, which Benjamin had already claimed for his own reign.

chapter.title: A vote decides a nation's border
chapter.text: The chief judge asks and the people answer. Mosiah 29 argued that the voice of the people usually chooses right, and this chapter is the case where it does.

chapter.title: The welcome comes with an invoice
chapter.text: Land, armies, and a levy, all in one sentence. Mormon reports the terms plainly and lets the reader decide what to make of a defense paid for by pacifists.

chapter.title: Joy is treated as a physical event
chapter.text: Ammon is swallowed up to the exhausting of his strength, and Mormon carefully notes that the other three were not. Alma 19 and Alma 22 had kings on the floor for the same reason.

chapter.title: They get a third name
chapter.text: Lamanites, then Anti-Nephi-Lehies, then the people of Ammon, given by Nephites and kept ever after. Each renaming marks a change in who they are attached to.

applications.title: Ask before you assume the answer
applications.text: The king was sure the Nephites would kill them, and Ammon proposed finding out. Where you are certain how someone will respond, consider that the certainty is untested and go test it.

applications.title: Refuse the payment someone offers out of guilt
applications.text: The king tried to buy asylum with his people's liberty, and Ammon said no on principle. When someone offers you far more than a wrong is worth, declining is part of the forgiveness.

applications.title: Put the hard question to the whole group
applications.text: The chief judge did not decide alone. Where a decision affects everyone and would be easier to make quietly, say it out loud and let people answer.

applications.title: State the conditions with the offer
applications.text: The Nephites promised protection and named the cost in the same breath. When you agree to help, say what you need in return at the time, so nobody discovers it later.

questions.text: What have I decided once that I would have to decide again if it were tested?
What am I sure I would be condemned for, and have I ever checked?
What am I overpaying for something I have already been forgiven?
Whose heart have I refused to try because I was afraid of the answer?
When did I last feel joy I would call too big for me?
What have I agreed to help with while leaving the cost unsaid?
What would change if I stopped looking at death with any degree of terror?
